items.title: DPSP — Nature, Source & Article 37
items.body:
## In one line

Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP) — guidelines in Part IV, Articles 36-51, that the government should follow but which courts cannot enforce.

## Why it is asked

Article 37's wording — 'not enforceable by any court' yet 'fundamental in the governance of the country' — is a repeat question.

The **Directive Principles of State Policy (DPSP)** are guidelines in **Part IV (Articles 36-51)** directing the State to establish a **social welfare state** securing social, economic and political justice. They were **borrowed from the Irish Constitution** (which took the idea from Spain) and embody the **Objectives Resolution** ideals.

Under **Article 37**, DPSP are **non-justiciable** — not enforceable by any court — yet **'fundamental in the governance of the country'**, and it is the duty of the State to apply them in making laws. They resemble the **'Instrument of Instructions'** issued to the Governor-General under the **Government of India Act, 1935**. Courts may use them as an **interpretive tool** to test the reasonableness of a law, and their real sanction is **political/moral** — accountability at the ballot box.

## Don't confuse

| Point | Fundamental Rights (Part III) | Directive Principles (Part IV) |
|---|---|---|
| Enforceable in court? | Yes (justiciable) | No (non-justiciable) |
| Addressed to | The State; some rights to all persons | The State only |
| Borrowed from | United States (bill of rights idea) | Ireland |

## Terms explained

- **DPSP (Directive Principles of State Policy)** — guidelines in Part IV that the State should follow but no court can enforce.
- **Non-justiciable** — not enforceable in a court of law.
- **Instrument of Instructions** — the standing directions given to the Governor-General under the 1935 Act, which the DPSP resemble.
- **Welfare state** — a state that actively promotes the social and economic well-being of its people.

## TL;DR

- DPSP are in Part IV, Articles 36-51, borrowed from the Irish Constitution (originally Spain).
- Article 37 — DPSP are non-justiciable but fundamental in governance; duty of State to apply them.
- They resemble the 'Instrument of Instructions' under the Government of India Act, 1935.
- Aim: shift from a police state to a welfare state; economic democracy alongside political democracy.
- Sanction is political/moral, not legal; courts use DPSP to judge a law's reasonableness.
keyPoints: DPSP are in Part IV, Articles 36-51, borrowed from the Irish Constitution (originally Spain).
Article 37 — DPSP are non-justiciable but fundamental in governance; duty of State to apply them.
They resemble the 'Instrument of Instructions' under the Government of India Act, 1935.
Aim: shift from a police state to a welfare state; economic democracy alongside political democracy.
Sanction is political/moral, not legal; courts use DPSP to judge a law's reasonableness.

items.title: Threefold Classification of DPSP
items.body:
## In one line

The DPSP are grouped into three types — Socialistic, Gandhian and Liberal-Intellectual.

## Why it is asked

Matching an Article to its category is a standard objective question.

Though the Constitution does not classify them, DPSP are conventionally grouped into three categories:

| Category | Basis | Key Articles |
|---|---|---|
| **Socialistic** | social & economic justice | 38 (justice, reduce inequality), 39 (right to an adequate means of livelihood; preventing concentration of wealth and means of production; equal pay for equal work for men and women), 39A (equal justice and free legal aid), 41 (work, education, public assistance), 42 (maternity relief), 43 (living wage), 43A (worker participation), 47 (nutrition & health) |
| **Gandhian** | Gandhi's ideals | 40 (organisation of village panchayats), 43 (promotion of cottage industries), 46 (SC/ST & weaker sections), 47 (prohibition of intoxicating drinks), 48 (cattle/cow slaughter) |
| **Liberal-Intellectual** | liberalism & science | 44 (Uniform Civil Code), 45 (early childhood care and education for children below six), 48 (modern agriculture), 48A (environment), 49 (monuments), 50 (separation of the judiciary from the executive in the public services), 51 (promotion of international peace) |

Note that some articles (for example, **47, 48, 43**) straddle categories.

**Don't confuse:** free and compulsory education is **NOT in Article 39** — it was Article 45 and, since the 86th Amendment (2002), is a Fundamental Right under **Article 21A**.

## Terms explained

- **Socialistic principles** — directives aimed at social and economic justice and reducing inequality.
- **Gandhian principles** — directives based on Gandhi’s ideals, such as village panchayats and cottage industries.
- **Liberal-Intellectual principles** — directives reflecting liberal and scientific ideas, such as a Uniform Civil Code and environmental protection.
- **UCC (Uniform Civil Code)** — one common set of personal laws for all citizens (Article 44).

## TL;DR

- Socialistic: Art 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47 — economic justice & equality.
- Gandhian: Art 40, 43, 46, 47, 48 — panchayats, cottage industries, prohibition, cattle.
- Liberal-Intellectual: Art 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51.
- Article 39: livelihood, prevention of concentration of wealth, equal pay for equal work.
- Article 44 = UCC; Article 50 = separation of judiciary from executive; Article 51 = international peace.
keyPoints: Socialistic: Art 38, 39, 39A, 41, 42, 43, 43A, 47 — economic justice & equality.
Gandhian: Art 40, 43, 46, 47, 48 — panchayats, cottage industries, prohibition, cattle.
Liberal-Intellectual: Art 44, 45, 48, 48A, 49, 50, 51.
Article 39: livelihood, prevention of concentration of wealth, equal pay for equal work.
Article 44 = UCC; Article 50 = separation of judiciary from executive; Article 51 = international peace.

items.title: New Directive Principles Added by Amendments
items.body:
## In one line

Several new Directive Principles were added later by amendments, and a few directives sit outside Part IV.

## Why it is asked

'Which amendment added which DPSP' is precise and frequently tested.

Later amendments enriched Part IV with new directives:

| Amendment | Addition |
|---|---|
| **42nd (1976)** | **Art 39A** (equal justice & free legal aid), **Art 43A** (participation of workers in management of industries), **Art 48A** (protection of environment, forests & wildlife) |
| **86th (2002)** | Recast **Art 45** to early childhood care & education for children below the age of six years; made free education for 6-14 a Fundamental Right under **Art 21A** |
| **97th (2011)** | **Art 43B** — promotion of voluntary formation, autonomous functioning and democratic control of **cooperative societies** |

There are also **directives outside Part IV**: **Art 335** (SC/ST claims to services), **Art 350A** (mother-tongue instruction at primary stage) and **Art 351** (development of the Hindi language).

## Terms explained

- **Amendment** — a formal change made to the Constitution under Article 368.
- **Cooperative societies** — member-owned, democratically run enterprises promoted by Article 43B.
- **Directives outside Part IV** — directive-type duties placed elsewhere, such as Articles 335, 350A and 351.

## TL;DR

- 42nd Amendment (1976) added Art 39A, 43A and 48A.
- 86th Amendment (2002) recast Art 45 (early childhood care) and made education a FR via Art 21A.
- 97th Amendment (2011) added Art 43B on cooperative societies.
- Directives outside Part IV: Art 335 (SC/ST services), Art 350A (mother tongue), Art 351 (Hindi).
keyPoints: 42nd Amendment (1976) added Art 39A, 43A and 48A.
86th Amendment (2002) recast Art 45 (early childhood care) and made education a FR via Art 21A.
97th Amendment (2011) added Art 43B on cooperative societies.
Directives outside Part IV: Art 335 (SC/ST services), Art 350A (mother tongue), Art 351 (Hindi).

items.title: Fundamental Rights vs DPSP — Evolution of Balance
items.body:
## In one line

This tracks the court battles over what happens when a Fundamental Right and a Directive Principle clash.

## Why it is asked

The Champakam to Golaknath to Kesavananda to Minerva Mills ladder is a favourite in both papers.

The relationship between Fundamental Rights (FR) and DPSP evolved through landmark cases:

| Case | Year | Holding |
|---|---|---|
| **Champakam Dorairajan** | 1951 | FR prevail over DPSP in conflict → led to 1st, 4th, 17th Amendments |
| **Golaknath** | 1967 | FR are 'sacrosanct' and cannot be amended to implement DPSP → prompted 24th & 25th Amendments |
| **Kesavananda Bharati** | 1973 | DPSP cannot override the **basic structure**; recognised the FR-DPSP balance |
| **Minerva Mills** | 1980 | Absolute primacy of DPSP over Art 14 & 19 would destroy the balance, which is itself part of the basic structure |

**Article 31C** (25th Amendment, 1971) was introduced to give certain Directive Principles primacy over Fundamental Rights: it protects laws implementing **Art 39(b)/(c)** from challenge under Art 14 and 19. The goal is **harmony** — FR and DPSP are complementary, not adversarial.

## Terms explained

- **Basic structure** — the core features of the Constitution that no amendment can destroy.
- **Article 31C** — a clause shielding laws that implement Article 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under Articles 14 and 19.
- **Harmony** — the settled position that Fundamental Rights and DPSP are complementary and must be read together.

## TL;DR

- Champakam Dorairajan (1951): FR prevail over DPSP → led to the 1st Amendment.
- Golaknath (1967): FR cannot be amended to enforce DPSP → led to 24th & 25th Amendments.
- Kesavananda Bharati (1973): DPSP cannot override the basic structure.
- Minerva Mills (1980): the FR-DPSP balance is part of the basic structure.
- Article 31C shields laws implementing Art 39(b)/(c) from Art 14 and 19.
keyPoints: Champakam Dorairajan (1951): FR prevail over DPSP → led to the 1st Amendment.
Golaknath (1967): FR cannot be amended to enforce DPSP → led to 24th & 25th Amendments.
Kesavananda Bharati (1973): DPSP cannot override the basic structure.
Minerva Mills (1980): the FR-DPSP balance is part of the basic structure.
Article 31C shields laws implementing Art 39(b)/(c) from Art 14 and 19.

items.title: Implementation, Utility & Criticism
items.body:
## In one line

How governments have actually turned the DPSP into real laws and schemes, and the main criticisms of the DPSP.

## Why it is asked

Linking a directive to a concrete law or scheme is tested in both papers.

**Implementation** — Key measures giving effect to DPSP: **land reform / zamindari abolition** (Art 39), **Minimum Wages Act 1948** and **Equal Remuneration Act 1976** (Art 39, 43), **nationalisation of banks & insurance**, **Panchayati Raj via the 73rd Amendment 1992** (Art 40), **MGNREGA 2005** (Art 41 right to work), protection of monuments and wildlife, and **NITI Aayog (2015)** replacing the Planning Commission for balanced development.

**Utility** — a yardstick for government performance; a framework for future legislation; ensures social justice and sustainable development.

**Criticism** — no legal force (non-justiciable); illogically arranged with no clear priority; can create Centre-State tension over implementation; conservative political philosophy in parts.

## Terms explained

- **Zamindari abolition** — ending the system of large intermediary landlords, to give land to tillers (Article 39).
- **MGNREGA (2005)** — a law guaranteeing rural households a set number of days of paid work (advances Article 41).
- **NITI Aayog (2015)** — the policy think-tank that replaced the Planning Commission to steer balanced development.

## TL;DR

- Land reforms, Minimum Wages Act (1948) and Equal Remuneration Act (1976) implement Art 39/43.
- MGNREGA (2005) advances Art 41 (right to work); 73rd Amendment (1992) implements Art 40.
- NITI Aayog (2015) replaced the Planning Commission for balanced development.
- Utility: yardstick for government performance and a framework for legislation.
- Criticism: no legal force, illogical arrangement, possible Centre-State tension.
keyPoints: Land reforms, Minimum Wages Act (1948) and Equal Remuneration Act (1976) implement Art 39/43.
MGNREGA (2005) advances Art 41 (right to work); 73rd Amendment (1992) implements Art 40.
NITI Aayog (2015) replaced the Planning Commission for balanced development.
Utility: yardstick for government performance and a framework for legislation.
Criticism: no legal force, illogical arrangement, possible Centre-State tension.

items.title: Every Directive Principle — Articles 36 to 51 Clause by Clause
items.body:
## Articles 36 to 51, one by one

**In one line:** Part IV is a list of goals the State must keep in view — each Article has a specific subject, and several clauses were added later by amendments.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC asks "concentration of wealth violates?" (39), "workers' participation added by?" (43A, 42nd), "international peace is in?" (51), and APPSC adds panchayats (40) and prohibition (47).

**The story**

### The Articles
| Article | Directive | Group |
|---|---|---|
| **36** | Definition of "**State**" — same as **Article 12** | — |
| **37** | DPSP **not enforceable** by any court but **fundamental in the governance** of the country; the State's **duty** to apply them in **making laws** | — |
| **38** | Promote **welfare** by securing a social order of **social, economic and political justice**; **38(2)** – minimise **inequalities in income**, status, facilities and opportunities (**44th Amendment, 1978**) | Socialistic |
| **39(a)** | Right to an **adequate means of livelihood** for all citizens | Socialistic |
| **39(b)** | Ownership and control of **material resources** distributed to serve the **common good** | Socialistic |
| **39(c)** | Prevent **concentration of wealth** and means of production | Socialistic |
| **39(d)** | **Equal pay for equal work** for men and women | Socialistic |
| **39(e)** | Protect the **health and strength of workers** and children against abuse | Socialistic |
| **39(f)** | Opportunities for the **healthy development of children** (**42nd Amendment**) | Socialistic |
| **39A** | **Equal justice** and **free legal aid** to the poor (**42nd Amendment**) | Socialistic |
| **40** | Organise **village panchayats** as units of self-government | **Gandhian** |
| **41** | Right to **work**, to **education** and to **public assistance** in unemployment, old age, sickness and disablement | Socialistic |
| **42** | **Just and humane conditions of work** and **maternity relief** | Socialistic |
| **43** | **Living wage** and decent standard of life for workers; promote **cottage industries** on an individual or co-operative basis in rural areas | Socialistic and **Gandhian** |
| **43A** | **Participation of workers in the management** of industries (**42nd Amendment**) | Socialistic |
| **43B** | Voluntary formation, autonomous functioning and democratic control of **co-operative societies** (**97th Amendment, 2011**) | Gandhian |
| **44** | **Uniform Civil Code** for citizens throughout India | Liberal-intellectual |
| **45** | **Early childhood care and education** for all children **below six** (recast by the **86th Amendment, 2002**; earlier: free and compulsory education up to **14**) | Liberal-intellectual |
| **46** | Promote the educational and economic interests of **SCs, STs and weaker sections** and protect them from social injustice | **Gandhian** |
| **47** | Raise the level of **nutrition**, standard of living and **public health**; **prohibit intoxicating drinks** and drugs injurious to health | Socialistic and **Gandhian** |
| **48** | Organise **agriculture and animal husbandry** on modern scientific lines; **prohibit the slaughter of cows**, calves and other milch and draught cattle | Gandhian and Liberal |
| **48A** | **Protect and improve the environment** and safeguard **forests and wildlife** (**42nd Amendment**) | Liberal-intellectual |
| **49** | Protect **monuments**, places and objects of artistic or historic interest declared of **national importance** | Liberal-intellectual |
| **50** | **Separate the judiciary from the executive** in the public services of the State | Liberal-intellectual |
| **51** | Promote **international peace and security**; just and honourable relations between nations; respect for **international law**; settle disputes by **arbitration** | Liberal-intellectual |

### Amendments that changed Part IV
| Amendment | Change |
|---|---|
| **42nd (1976)** | Added **39(f)**, **39A**, **43A** and **48A** — four changes |
| **44th (1978)** | Added **38(2)** — minimise inequalities in income |
| **86th (2002)** | Recast **Article 45** (early childhood care below six); education for 6–14 moved to **Article 21A** |
| **97th (2011)** | Added **Article 43B** (co-operative societies) |

## Don't confuse
- **39(b)/(c)** = resources for the common good / no concentration of wealth — these are the clauses **Article 31C** protects.
- **Article 43 = living wage + cottage industries; 43A = workers in management; 43B = co-operatives.**
- **Article 48 = agriculture and cattle; 48A = environment, forests, wildlife.**
- **Article 45 today = children below six**, not up to 14.

**TL;DR**
- 36 State (= Article 12); 37 non-justiciable but fundamental in governance.
- 38 welfare, 38(2) inequalities (44th); 39(a)-(f): livelihood, resources, no concentration of wealth, equal pay, workers' health, children (39(f) 42nd); 39A legal aid.
- 40 panchayats; 41 work/education/assistance; 42 maternity relief; 43 living wage and cottage industries; 43A workers in management; 43B co-operatives.
- 44 UCC; 45 below six; 46 SC/ST; 47 nutrition and prohibition; 48 agriculture and cows; 48A environment; 49 monuments; 50 separation of judiciary; 51 international peace.
keyPoints: Article 36 defines 'State' as in Article 12; Article 37 says DPSP are not enforceable but fundamental in governance and must be applied in making laws.
Article 38(2), added by the 44th Amendment (1978), directs the State to minimise inequalities in income, status, facilities and opportunities.

Article 39: (a) livelihood, (b) material resources for the common good, (c) no concentration of wealth, (d) equal pay for equal work, (e) health of workers, (f) healthy development of children (42nd Amendment).
Article 41 – right to work, education and public assistance; Article 42 – just and humane conditions of work and maternity relief; Article 43 – living wage and cottage industries.
Article 46 – interests of SCs, STs and weaker sections; Article 47 – nutrition, public health and prohibition; Article 48 – agriculture, animal husbandry and cow-slaughter ban.
Article 49 – monuments of national importance; Article 50 – separation of judiciary from executive; Article 51 – international peace, international law and arbitration.
The 42nd Amendment made four changes: 39(f), 39A, 43A and 48A.

items.title: Nature of the DPSP — Origin, Quotes, Directives Outside Part IV & Criticism
items.body:
## What kind of provisions the DPSP are

**In one line:** the DPSP are positive instructions to the State — borrowed from Ireland, unenforceable in court, but meant to build social and economic democracy.

**Why it is asked:** UPSC 2017 asked whether DPSP limit legislative and executive functions (they do not); state PSCs ask "who called the DPSP a cheque payable at the convenience of the bank?".

**The story**

### Origin and nature
- The **Sapru Committee (1945)** suggested two kinds of rights — **justiciable** (became Fundamental Rights) and **non-justiciable** (became DPSP).
- Borrowed from the **Irish Constitution (1937)**, which had copied the idea from the **Spanish** Constitution.
- They resemble the **Instrument of Instructions** issued to the Governor-General and Governors under the **GoI Act 1935** — but given to the legislature and executive.
- They aim at a **welfare state**, not a **police state**; they spell out **social and economic democracy**, while FRs give **political democracy**.
- They are **positive directions** to the State; they are **not limitations** on its legislative or executive powers (UPSC 2017).
- Courts may use them to judge the **reasonableness** of a law; their **sanction** is **moral and political** — the voters.
- The Constitution itself does **not classify** them; the socialistic/Gandhian/liberal-intellectual grouping is by scholars.

### What people said
| Person | Remark on the DPSP |
|---|---|
| **B.R. Ambedkar** | A "**novel feature**" of the Constitution |
| **Granville Austin** | Together with FRs, the "**conscience of the Constitution**" |
| **K.T. Shah** | "A **cheque on a bank**, payable at the **convenience of the bank**" |
| **Nasiruddin** | Like "**New Year's Day resolutions**" broken on 2 January |
| **T.T. Krishnamachari** | "A veritable **dustbin of sentiments**" |
| **Ivor Jennings** | "**Pious aspirations**" |
| **K.C. Wheare** | A "**manifesto of aims and aspirations**" |

### Directives outside Part IV
| Article | Directive |
|---|---|
| **335** (Part XVI) | Claims of **SCs and STs** to services, consistent with efficiency of administration |
| **350A** (Part XVII) | Instruction in the **mother tongue** at the **primary** stage for linguistic minority children |
| **351** (Part XVII) | Promote the spread and development of the **Hindi** language |
- These are **non-justiciable** too, but the courts treat them like Part IV directives.

### FR vs DPSP — the full contrast
| Point | Fundamental Rights | Directive Principles |
|---|---|---|
| Nature | **Negative** — stop the State doing some things | **Positive** — ask the State to do things |
| Enforceable | **Justiciable** | **Non-justiciable** |
| Aim | **Political democracy** | **Social and economic democracy** |
| Legal sanction | Courts can **strike down** a law that violates them | Courts **cannot** strike down a law for violating them |
| Promote | **Individual** welfare | **Community** welfare |
| Need laws? | **Automatically** enforced | Need **legislation** to be implemented |

### Criticism and utility
- **Criticism:** **no legal force**; **illogically arranged** with no consistent philosophy; **conservative** in parts (from the 19th-century England model); may cause **constitutional conflict** between the Centre and the states, between the President and the PM, and between a Governor and a CM.
- **Utility:** they are a **yardstick** to judge government performance; a **framework** for future legislation; they fill gaps in Part III; they help courts interpret laws; they serve **social justice, economic equality** and **sustainable development**; and they supplement FRs.

## Don't confuse
- **K.T. Shah = cheque on a bank; T.T. Krishnamachari = dustbin of sentiments; Nasiruddin = New Year's resolutions.**
- **Sapru Committee (1945)** split rights into justiciable/non-justiciable — not the Swaran Singh Committee (Fundamental Duties).

**TL;DR**
- Sapru Committee 1945; Irish 1937 (from Spain); like the Instrument of Instructions (1935 Act).
- Positive directions, not limitations; social and economic democracy; moral and political sanction.
- Quotes: Ambedkar novel; Austin conscience; K.T. Shah cheque; Nasiruddin New Year; TTK dustbin; Jennings pious aspirations.
- Outside Part IV: 335 (SC/ST services), 350A (mother tongue), 351 (Hindi).
- Criticism: no legal force, illogical, conservative, conflict; utility: yardstick, framework, interpretation.
keyPoints: The Sapru Committee (1945) proposed justiciable and non-justiciable rights; DPSP came from the Irish Constitution (1937), which borrowed from Spain.
DPSP are positive directions and not limitations on the legislative or executive functions of the State (UPSC 2017).
DPSP aim at social and economic democracy and a welfare state; FRs secure political democracy.
Austin called FRs and DPSP the 'conscience of the Constitution'; K.T. Shah 'a cheque on a bank payable at the convenience of the bank'; T.T. Krishnamachari 'a veritable dustbin of sentiments'.
Ivor Jennings called DPSP 'pious aspirations'; Nasiruddin compared them to New Year's Day resolutions.
Directives outside Part IV: Article 335 (SC/ST claims to services), 350A (mother tongue at primary stage), 351 (development of Hindi).
Courts cannot strike down a law for violating a DPSP; DPSP need legislation, FRs are automatically enforced.

items.title: FR–DPSP Conflict & Implementation — Amendments, Cases and Laws
items.body:
## How the conflict was settled, and how DPSP became laws

**In one line:** courts first put Fundamental Rights above the DPSP; Parliament answered with amendments; the Supreme Court finally said both must be balanced — and Parliament has turned many directives into laws.

**Why it is asked:** the case–amendment chain (Champakam → 1st Amendment; Golaknath → 24th/25th; Kesavananda → 31C; Minerva → balance) and "which law implements which Article" are recurring items.

**The story**

### The conflict, step by step
| Step | What happened |
|---|---|
| **Champakam Dorairajan (1951)** | FRs **prevail** over DPSP; DPSP must run as **subsidiary** to FRs → Parliament passed the **1st (1951), 4th (1955) and 17th (1964) Amendments** |
| **Golaknath (1967)** | FRs are **sacrosanct**; Parliament cannot amend them to implement DPSP |
| **24th Amendment (1971)** | Declared that Parliament **can amend any part** of the Constitution, including FRs |
| **25th Amendment (1971)** | Inserted **Article 31C** — laws for **39(b) and 39(c)** cannot be challenged under **Articles 14 and 19** (original text also cited 31) and courts could not examine whether the law really served the policy |
| **Kesavananda Bharati (1973)** | Upheld 31C's **first part**; struck down the **second part** (exclusion of judicial review) |
| **42nd Amendment (1976)** | Extended 31C to **all** Directive Principles |
| **Minerva Mills (1980)** | Struck down that extension; the Constitution rests on a **balance** between FRs and DPSP, which is part of the **basic structure**; DPSP of 39(b)/(c) may prevail over 14 and 19 only |

- **Present position:** FRs have **primacy** in general, but laws giving effect to **39(b) and (c)** are protected from **Articles 14 and 19**. The two are **complementary** — Parliament may amend FRs to implement DPSP as long as the basic structure is untouched.

### Implementation — directive → law
| Directive | Law / step |
|---|---|
| **39** (resources, wealth) | **Land reforms** — abolition of **zamindari**, ceilings on holdings; **nationalisation** of banks (1969) and insurance |
| **39(d), 43** (equal pay, wages) | **Minimum Wages Act 1948**; **Equal Remuneration Act 1976** (now the Code on Wages 2019) |
| **39A** (legal aid) | **Legal Services Authorities Act 1987** — NALSA, Lok Adalats |
| **40** (panchayats) | **73rd Amendment 1992** — constitutional status to Panchayati Raj |
| **41** (right to work) | **MGNREGA 2005** — 100 days of wage employment (the source dates the scheme 2006, when it began) |
| **42** (maternity relief) | **Maternity Benefit Act 1961** (amended 2017 — 26 weeks) |
| **43** (cottage industries) | **Khadi and Village Industries Commission**, handloom and small-industry boards |
| **45** (early childhood) | **ICDS (1975)** — anganwadis |
| **47** (nutrition, prohibition) | **Mid-day meal** (PM POSHAN); **prohibition** laws in states such as **Gujarat** and **Bihar** |
| **48A** (environment) | **Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972**; **Forest (Conservation) Act 1980**; **Environment (Protection) Act 1986** |
| **49** (monuments) | **Ancient Monuments and Archaeological Sites and Remains Act 1958** |
| **50** (separation of judiciary) | **Criminal Procedure Code 1973** separated judicial from executive magistrates |
| **44** (UCC) | **Goa** has long had a common civil code; **Uttarakhand** brought its **Uniform Civil Code** into force on **27 January 2025** — the first state to enact one after independence |
- The source also lists **NITI Aayog (2015)**, which replaced the Planning Commission, as a step towards balanced development.

### Andhra Pradesh angle
- **Article 47 (prohibition):** the N.T. Rama Rao government imposed **total prohibition** in **Andhra Pradesh** in **January 1995**; it was **lifted in 1997**.
- **Article 40 (panchayats):** Andhra Pradesh adopted the three-tier Panchayati Raj in **1959**, right after **Rajasthan** (Nagaur, 2 October 1959).

## Don't confuse
- **24th = Parliament can amend FRs; 25th = Article 31C.**
- **Kesavananda struck only 31C's second part; Minerva struck the 42nd Amendment's extension.**
- **Article 50 → CrPC 1973; Article 39A → Legal Services Authorities Act 1987.**

**TL;DR**
- Champakam 1951 (FR prevail) → 1st, 4th, 17th Amendments; Golaknath 1967 → 24th and 25th (31C, 1971).
- Kesavananda 1973: 31C part 1 valid, part 2 void; 42nd extended 31C; Minerva 1980: balance is basic structure.
- Laws: Minimum Wages 1948; Equal Remuneration 1976; Legal Services 1987; MGNREGA 2005; Maternity Benefit 1961; Wildlife 1972; Monuments 1958; CrPC 1973.
- UCC: Goa; Uttarakhand from 27 January 2025. AP: prohibition 1995–97; panchayats 1959.
keyPoints: After Champakam Dorairajan (1951) Parliament passed the 1st (1951), 4th (1955) and 17th (1964) Amendments.
The 24th Amendment (1971) affirmed Parliament's power to amend FRs; the 25th Amendment (1971) inserted Article 31C for 39(b) and 39(c).
Kesavananda Bharati upheld the first part of 31C and struck down its second part; the 42nd Amendment extended 31C to all DPSPs, which Minerva Mills struck down.
Article 39A is implemented by the Legal Services Authorities Act 1987; Article 42 by the Maternity Benefit Act 1961; Article 50 by the CrPC 1973.
Article 48A: Wildlife (Protection) Act 1972, Forest (Conservation) Act 1980, Environment (Protection) Act 1986; Article 49: Ancient Monuments Act 1958.
Uttarakhand brought its Uniform Civil Code into force on 27 January 2025; Goa already had a common civil code.
Andhra Pradesh imposed total prohibition in January 1995 (Article 47), lifted in 1997.

items.title: For Mains — Directive Principles of State Policy
items.body:
## Why Mains asks this (Paper-III, Polity & Governance; clauses M3-1, M3-15a)

DPSP answers reward the **FR-DPSP balance, the welfare-state argument, and implementation-vs-criticism**, not article-listing.

| Dimension | What to deploy |
|---|---|
| **Nature** | Non-justiciable (Art 37) but 'fundamental in governance'; 'Instrument of Instructions' (GoI Act 1935) |
| **Classification** | Socialistic (38, 39, 41, 43, 47), Gandhian (40, 43, 46, 47, 48), Liberal-Intellectual (44, 45, 48A, 50, 51) |
| **FR-DPSP balance** | Champakam (1951) → Golaknath (1967) → Kesavananda (1973) → Minerva Mills (1980, balance = basic structure) |
| **Implementation** | Land reforms, Minimum Wages Act 1948, Equal Remuneration Act 1976, MGNREGA 2005, 73rd/74th Amdts, RTE 2009 |
| **Criticism** | No legal force, illogically arranged, no priority, Centre-State friction, conservative in parts |
| **Way forward** | Make key directives justiciable incrementally (as with RTE → Art 21A); outcome budgeting; SDG alignment |

**Data / authorities to quote:** Granville Austin called FR and DPSP the Constitution's 'conscience'; Minerva Mills (1980) 'harmony and balance'; Art 31C (25th Amendment, 1971); Uttarakhand UCC (in force 27 Jan 2025) as a live Art 44 instance; MGNREGA (Art 41); NITI Aayog (2015) and SDG localisation as modern welfare-state tools.

**AP angle:** AP operationalises DPSP through mandal-level Panchayati Raj (Art 40), welfare and nutrition schemes (Art 47 — for example, midday meals, PDS), women-focused SHG/DWCRA programmes (Art 39/46), and legal-aid machinery (Art 39A); the state's heavy welfare-scheme orientation after bifurcation is a textbook DPSP illustration.

**Use in answers:** frame DPSP and FR as 'two wheels of the chariot of justice'; use the four-case ladder for the balance question; pair each classification with one concrete scheme to show application; close with 'the UCC and RTE show directives maturing into enforceable rights'. A three-circle classification diagram adds structure.
keyPoints: Argue the welfare state via Art 37 and the Socialistic/Gandhian/Liberal classification with concrete schemes.
Use Champakam → Golaknath → Kesavananda → Minerva Mills for the FR-DPSP balance (basic structure).
Quote Granville Austin's 'conscience of the Constitution' and Minerva Mills' 'harmony and balance'.
Cite implementation: land reforms, wage laws, MGNREGA (Art 41), 73rd/74th Amdts (Art 40), RTE 2009.
Use Uttarakhand UCC (in force Jan 2025) as a live Article 44 example; note DPSP maturing into rights.
AP angle: mandal Panchayati Raj, welfare/nutrition schemes, SHG/DWCRA, legal aid as DPSP in practice.
